newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Shaba political leader urges Mobutu-Kabila talks.
newsitem.headline: Shaba political leader urges Mobutu-Kabila talks.

text.p: The leading politician in Zaire's mineral-rich Shaba region urged rebel leader Laurent Kabila on Saturday to agree to a peace initiative from his foe, President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Mobutu, weak after cancer treatment in Europe, returned home on Friday after proposing a National Council to end the five-month civil war and chart a future for the vast, chaotic Central African republic.

Kyungu wa Kumwanza, Shaba's suspended governor and leader of the major pro-autonomy opposition party, UFERI, said the Council met his own demand that peace talks must include regional powers like himself, not just Kabila and Mobutu.

"If I have a message for Kabila now it is that he must talk to Mobutu, the only solution is that they meet," he told Reuters at his home in Zaire's second city Lubumbashi, some 1,700 km (1,050 miles) southeast of the capital Kinshasa.

Kabila, who long demanded face-to-face talks with Mobutu before any ceasefire, said this week after taking the prized jungle city of Kisangani that only talks on the president's resignation could now bring a truce.

Despite his opposition status, some critics associate Kyungu, governor until 1995, with the corruption and self-enrichment that has characterised Mobutu's three decades in power and left a potentially rich country in rags.
His name is on a widely publicised list, supposedly drawn up by Kabila, of people the rebels will not cooperate with.

However, Kyungu and his party are the strongest political force in Shaba, or Katanga as they call it. They say Shaba's copper, cobalt and other precious minerals have the potential -- squandered under Mobutu's chaotic rule -- to make it wealthy.

U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun flew to Kisangani on Saturday for talks with Kabila, which Kyungu said was a sign that Paris and Washington, long divided over Zaire, had now agreed to pressure him for peace.
Diplomats said Sahnoun was believed to be carrying a special message and proposals for a ceasefire.
A political source said Kabila was coming under heavy pressure to stop fighting, especially after Mobutu's latest proposals, the first time he had agreed to talk to the rebels.
"He now risks being labelled 'the bad boy' if he continues to refuse to do so," the source said.
Kabila's forces have taken the north of Shaba -- his home province -- and are about 400 km (250 miles) from its capital Lubumbashi, their positions little changed since a week ago.
Last weekend, a wave of panic swept the city after Kabila, basking in the glory of his fresh conquest of Kisangani, declared Lubumbashi, home to a million people, his next goal.
Since then he seems to have changed his mind, declaring that Kinshasa and the diamond capital Mbuji-Mayi were next.

Lubumbashi, whose people say they are waiting for Kabila with open arms, has calmed since then. The main fear, of looting by Zairean soldiers before they flee, has eased since commanders apparently disarmed more volatile army units.
